notes.text: By a plumb-line — Strongly and beautifully built.
Set a plumb-line — I will exactly measure the whole ten tribes. Pass by them - I will no more forbear, but will pull down all that is faulty.
The high places — The temples on high mountains built to idols. Of Isaac - The seed of Isaac.
In the midst — Openly, and publickly, endeavouring to stir up Israel to sedition or rebellion. The land - The people cannot bear all his harsh predictions.
Jeroboam shall die — He nowhere said so, but spake of his house distinguished from his person, as ver. 9.
The king's court — To which therefore thou oughtest to shew more respect, and not thus to affront the king in his own house.

No prophet — Not originally, or by study, or by any human designation. An herdman - By breeding and occupation I was and still am, an herdman. Sycamore fruit - This fruit was good food for man, or cattle.
The house of Isaac — The posterity of Isaac.

In a polluted land — Among the Heathen. Israel - The ten tribes. The vision of a basket of summer fruit, ver. 1-3. The destruction of the oppressors foretold, ver. 4-10. And a famine of the word of God, ver. 11-14.

Standeth — To observe all that is said or done there. Mighty - Kings or chief rulers. By their congregation he understands all persons whatsoever of this high and sacred order. Judgeth - Passes sentence upon them. The gods - Judges and magistrates are called gods, because they have their commission from God, and act as his deputies.
How long — The psalmist speaks to them in God's name. Accept - By giving sentence according to your respect or affection to the person.

They — The magistrates of whom this psalm treats. Know not - The duty of their place. Nor will - Their ignorance is wilful. Walk on - They persist: it is their constant course. In darkness - In their sinful courses. The foundations - This corruption of the supreme rulers, flows from them to their inferior officers and members.

Have said — I have given you my name and power to rule your people in my stead. All - Not only the rulers of Israel, but of all other nations. Children - Representing my person, and bearing both my name and authority.
Like men — Or, like ordinary men.

Arise — Take the sword of justice into thine own hand. A remonstrance of the designs and endeavours of Israel's enemies, ver. 1-8. A prayer, that God would defeat them, preserve his church, and get himself glory, ver. 9-18. A song or psalm of Asaph.

glossa.text: *A psalm of Asaph.* ((CASS.)) A psalm on the two natures in Christ, in which Christ, or the Prophet speaking, reproaches Asaph himself, that is, the Synagogue, which saw the Lord bodily, and yet did not know him. First he announces that God has stood, and convicts the adversaries: man stands, God discerns. *God hath stood.* Whose part it is not to stand, who filleth heaven and earth, who is within all things not enclosed, outside all things not excluded; but briefly he indicates God as man. *He hath stood.* ((AUG.)) The Son, who was sent to the sheep of the house of Israel; but the spiritual presence of the Godhead, which, being everywhere, does not properly belong to the Synagogue, nor is varied by time. Why he stood there: *Behold, he judgeth gods,* that is, according as he is God, that is, not by merits but by grace he distinguishes the vessels, some unto honour, some unto dishonour. But this he does standing in the midst, whence: *There hath stood one in the midst of you, whom you know not,* whence also here: *They have not known, neither have they understood,* but *the friend of the bridegroom standeth and heareth, and rejoiceth with joy. Of gods.* Whom afterwards he calls *sons of the Most High,* there: *I have said: you are gods, and all of you to the sons of the Most High.* Whence also, *I have brought up children and exalted them, but they have despised me.* They are called sons not only by the grace of the New Testament, but by the grace of the Old, which delivered them out of Egypt.

*How long.* ((AUG.)) This is the voice of him that discerneth: he sent the law and the Prophets, and you resisted; but how long? Did I send Prophets until the coming, and you afflicted them with injuries, or slew them, or consented to those who did this? But since it is not worthy even to speak to those who do such things, you who kept silence, and wished to imitate them, *how long do you judge iniquity, and accept the persons of sinners?* Is the heir also to be slain, who came for you, who for your sake willed to be without a father, as a fatherless child? who for your sake hungered and thirsted, as a needy man, who for your sake was made poor, when he was rich.

*Judge for the needy and the fatherless, justify the poor and the humble.* ((CASS.)) Diapsalma, he admonishes that one should understand Christ to be God, even if he was needy and poor, which he says that they did not do.

*Rescue the poor.* ((AUG.)) He shows that not even those are guiltless who left Christ to the princes, since they were feared on account of their multitude, and could have freed them from the deed, and themselves from consent. ((CASS.)) For he who ceases to withstand when he can, consents.

*They shall be moved.* ((CASS.)) Hence it is plain of whom he had spoken: this sign happened at the crucifixion. Or spiritually, earthly men were moved at that time, so great a miracle being seen; as the centurion, who said: *Indeed this was the Son of God.* ((AUG.)) *All the foundations shall be moved.* As if he should say: through this blindness of Israel, *shall be moved* unto faith *all the foundations of the earth,* that is, the fulness of the Gentiles shall come in. Or, in the death and passion of the Lord the earth was moved. Or *the foundations,* that is, those made happy by abundance of earthly things, shall be moved. Or by wondering that a poor dead man is worshipped. Or by following after him, earthly things being despised. He adds *all,* because there is none who does not wonder, or is not converted. But the kingdom of earthly felicity is pride, against which the humble Christ came, reproaching them whom he wills to make high through humility, in these words: *I have said: you are gods,* you the good: *but you* the evil, *shall die like men.* Or he says to all: *you are gods,* that is, to all I promised heavenly things; *but you as men,* the first men, who sinned by persuasion, and you greater ones as the devil, who by pride sinned.

*I have said.* ((CASS.)) What was set before them? but they perished. *I have said: They have not known, neither have they understood;* yet *I have said.* All receive these promises, if they keep the commandments, that they may be sons, and of God: this to the just; *but you,* this to the wicked.

*Like men.* ((AUG.)) As if: Whereas you are quickly to die, like men, you are not corrected thereby; but like the devil, who dies not in the flesh, you are lifted up, that you may fall: because through diabolical pride they envied the glory of Christ, and the humility of the cross became vile to them. But, that this vice may be healed, there is subjoined in the person of the Prophet: *Arise, O God,* etc., *as one.* The crowd which fell is called one, because it is alike in pride: You shall fall, but:
*Arise, O God.* ((AUG.)) That is, condemn these, because, these being cast off, thou shalt inherit. Or judge the world, because it is thine, and this is: thou shalt inherit.

notes.text: Commends the knowledge of Christ, as more excellent than all other, and so entire and perfect that no other knowledge was necessary for a Christian. He shows,

That Christ is above all angels, who are only his servants; and that, being reconciled to God through him, we have free access to him in all our necessities. This epistle contains, I. The inscription, Chap. i. 1, 2 II. The doctrine, wherein the apostle pathetically explains the mystery of Christ, By thanksgiving for the Colossians, 3-8 By prayers for them, 9-23 With a declaration of his affection for them, 24-29 ii. 1-3 III. The exhortation,

1. General, wherein he excites them to perseverance, and warns them not to be deceived, 4-8 Describes again the mystery of Christ in order, 9-15 And in the same order, draws his admonitions,

1. From Christ the head, 16-19

2. From his death, 20-23

3. From his exaltation, iii. 1-4

2. Particular, 5-9

1. To avoid several vices,

2. To practice several virtues, 10, 11 Especially to love one another, 12-15 And study the scriptures 16, 17

3. To the relative duties of wives and husbands,. 18, 19 Children and parents, 20, 21 Servants and masters, 22-25 iv.1 Final, to prayer, 2-4 to spiritual wisdom 5, 6 V. The conclusion, 7-16 COLOSSIANS
We give thanks — There is a near resemblance between this epistle, and those to the Ephesians and Philippians.
Ye heard before — I wrote to you. In the word of truth, of the gospel - The true gospel preached to you.
It bringeth forth fruit in all the world — That is, in every place where it is preached. Ye knew the grace of God in truth - Truly experienced the gracious power of God.
The fellowservant — Of Paul and Timotheus.
Your love in the Spirit — Your love wrought in you by the Spirit.

We pray for you — This was mentioned in general, Colossians i, 3, but now more particularly. That ye may be filled with the knowledge of his will - Of his revealed will. In all wisdom - With all the wisdom from above. And spiritual understanding - To discern by that light whatever agrees with, or differs from, his will.

That, knowing his whole will, ye may walk worthy of the Lord, unto all pleasing — So as actually to please him in all things; daily increasing in the living, experimental knowledge of God, our Father, saviour, Sanctifier.

Strengthened unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness — This is the highest point: not only to know, to do, to suffer, the whole will of God; but to suffer it to the end, not barely with patience, but with thankful joy.
Who, by justifying and sanctifying us, hath made us meet for glory.
Power detains reluctant captives, a kingdom cherishes willing subjects. His beloved Son — This is treated of in the fifteenth and following verses.

In whom we have redemption — This is treated of from the middle of Colossians i, 18. The voluntary passion of our Lord appeased the Father's wrath, obtained pardon and acceptance for us, and, consequently, dissolved the dominion and power which Satan had over us through our sins. So that forgiveness is the beginning of redemption, as the resurrection is the completion of it.

glossa.text: *Paul.* After his custom he sets the salutation first. This being set first, he gives thanks for their good things, and, commending their faith and love, he prays that they may be made perfect in Christ, whose benefits and primacy he commends according to both natures; then, calling to mind the dignity of his own ministry, he admonishes them not to withdraw from Christ, seduced through prophecy or the ceremonies of the law; last of all he instructs all together, morally, according to sexes and ages and conditions, and at the end he warns Archippus that he is to be careful of the ministry he has undertaken. *An apostle,* etc. Note that to all in dignity he here rightly names himself an apostle, because he was an apostle to these also, to whom he had preached through his own disciples.
*We give thanks.* He shows the good things which they received, while he gives thanks for them.

*As,* etc. That is, so purely and truly as it came through me and others into the whole world, and still remains in it, as if he should say: Not less has been done for you than in the other churches. Since the Gospel is in the world, it bears fruit there through good works, and grows by the increase of knowledge and by the number of the faithful. Not by this do they have more than you, but God does this in the same manner as it is among you, and therefore you ought to add nothing further.
*For you,* etc. Desiring whose salvation, he began to help Archippus.
*In the Spirit.* Because you love for spiritual things, not for carnal.
*That you may be filled in all.* It is a great thing to know fully what God wills, in all the matters of the active and the contemplative life.
*In knowledge.* That they may not be ignorant of the form of their faith, that is, of the thing hoped for, whence they will be firm.

*In all virtue.* You, I say, strengthened by God in all virtue, namely chastity and the rest. Which he can well do who is the brightness of the Father, that is, the Son. Or according as he has given you clear knowledge.

*Giving thanks.* Now he begins to say that the law does not profit but harms, and that Christ suffices for all good things: which can be known from this, that he himself and the other apostles (who had been in the observances of the law), having dismissed them, fled for refuge to Christ: As if he should say: We pray for you, giving thanks to God, for this reason, because he makes us worthy, which the law never could.

 *He has made us worthy.* Not in the law, but *in the light,* that is, through God who is light of light, by whose grace we are illumined. Or *in the light,* that is, in clear knowledge, from which he who turns aside falls into darkness. *Of the lot.* The will of God is the lot in the human race, with whom there is no iniquity, but he does all things by justice, though a hidden one.

*He has snatched us from the power.* That is, from hell, in which we were held by the devil: as much from our own transgression as from Adam's. *And has translated,* etc. When, raising us from the depth of Tartarus, he brought us into heaven with his only Son. For now believers, who are devoted with fixed mind, going forth from the world, are brought into heaven with an angel of the Father's right hand for their guide. *The kingdom of the Son.* Of which he himself says: *My kingdom is not of this world;* he did not say: It is not here, but, *it is not hence,* because he does indeed sojourn in the world, but is not of the world. For to his own kingdom he says, *You are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world.* They were of the world, when they belonged to the prince of the world.

*Redemption.* The power of the devil being destroyed, the means of liberty was given to us by the pouring out of the blood of him who had no sin. So that, because the devil justly held those whom, guilty of sin, he had bound by the condition of death, he might justly let these go through him whom, guilty of no sin, the punishment of death undeservedly visited.

notes.text: Matt. xxii, 35; Mark xii, 28.

Thou shalt love the Lord thy God — That is, thou shalt unite all the faculties of thy soul to render him the most intelligent and sincere, the most affectionate and resolute service. We may safely rest in this general sense of these important words, if we are not able to fix the particular meaning of every single word. If we desire to do this, perhaps the heart, which is a general expression, may be explained by the three following, With all thy soul, with the warmest affection, with all thy strength, the most vigourous efforts of thy will, and with all thy mind or understanding, in the most wise and reasonable manner thou canst; thy understanding guiding thy will and affections. Deut. vi, 5; Lev. xix, 18.

Thou hast answered right; this do, and thou shalt live — Here is no irony, but a deep and weighty truth. He, and he alone, shall live forever, who thus loves God and his neighbour in the present life.
To justify himself — That is, to show he had done this. Lev. xviii, 5.

From Jerusalem to Jericho — The road from Jerusalem to Jericho (about eighteen miles from it) lay through desert and rocky places: so many robberies and murders were committed therein, that it was called the bloody way. Jericho was situated in the valley: hence the phrase of going down to it. About twelve thousand priests and Levites dwelt there, who all attended the service of the temple.

The common translation is, by chance — Which is full of gross improprieties. For if we speak strictly, there is no such thing in the universe as either chance or fortune. A certain priest came down that way, and passed by on the other side - And both he and the Levite no doubt could find an excuse for passing over on the other side, and might perhaps gravely thank God for their own deliverance, while they left their brother bleeding to death. Is it not an emblem of many living characters, perhaps of some who bear the sacred office? O house of Levi and of Aaron, is not the day coming, when the virtues of heathens and Samaritans will rise up in judgment against you?

But a certain Samaritan came where he was — It was admirably well judged to represent the distress on the side of the Jew, and the mercy on that of the Samaritan. For the case being thus proposed, self interest would make the very scribe sensible, how amiable such a conduct was, and would lay him open to our Lord's inference. Had it been put the other way, prejudice might more easily have interposed, before the heart could have been affected.
Pouring in oil and wine — Which when well beaten together are one of the best balsams that can be applied to a fresh wound.
Which of these was the neighbour to him that fell among the robbers — Which acted the part of a neighbour?

And he said, He that showed mercy on him — He could not for shame say otherwise, though he thereby condemned himself and overthrew his own false notion of the neighbour to whom our love is due. Go and do thou in like manner - Let us go and do likewise, regarding every man as our neighbour who needs our assistance. Let us renounce that bigotry and party zeal which would contract our hearts into an insensibility for all the human race, but a small number whose sentiments and practices are so much our own, that our love to them is but self love reflected. With an honest openness of mind let us always remember that kindred between man and man, and cultivate that happy instinct whereby, in the original constitution of our nature, God has strongly bound us to each other.

glossa.text: *A lawyer stood up.* The doctor of the law, who was lying in the law without faith, rises that he may stand: he stands while he calls him Master, but even in standing he tempts God by keeping silent about what he was.
*He answering said.* He said what he had read, but did not fulfil what was written, because he had present with him the Lord whom he ought to love, yet he calls him Master, not God.

*But he, willing.* The lawyer, that he may be said to have answered wisely, first confesses that he is ignorant of the commandment of the law, because, refusing to be humbled and willing to justify himself, he cannot see the hidden things that are revealed to the little ones of Christ; to whom Christ so tempers his answer that both everyone who does mercy may be understood to be a neighbour, and especially the Son of God himself, who through his humanity has been made neighbour to us, may be designated. *Who is my.* No one is nearer to man than God, who knows him within and without and can care for all things; but every unbeliever or tempter has neither God nor man for a neighbour.

*A certain man,* etc. ((AUG.)) That man is understood to be Adam in the human race, etc., *as far as* he was nearer than the priest or the Levite of the same nation.

*And it happened,* etc. The priest announces the law of God: the law indeed came down through Moses into the world, and conferred no health upon such a one. The Levite came down, who shows the type of the prophets, but he too heals no one, because the law reproves sins, but passes by, since it does not bestow pardon.
*Being moved with mercy.* This is not said of the priest and the Levite, because the law has not mercy, but judgment and vengeance.
*He brought him to an inn.* He calls it not a house but a stable, by which name he marks the miseries and the stenches of this life, lest a man rejoice in this exile as though in his fatherland.
*He that did.* Kinship does not make a neighbour, but mercy, which mercy is according to nature. For nothing is so according to nature as to help a partner of one's nature.

echoes.text: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The epistolary blessing 'Grace to you and peace' channels the Aaronic benediction's pairing of divine favor and shalom (the LORD make his face shine... and give you peace). Volume is low and the formula is conventionally Pauline, but the coherence with the priestly grace/peace dyad and its availability in the Torah make it a plausible faint figural backdrop.

echoes.text: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
echoes.note: The gospel 'bearing fruit and growing... in all the world' (v.6) replays the creation/Edenic mandate 'be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.' The paired participles fruit-bearing + increasing, set worldwide, deliberately recast the protological blessing as the spread of the word, a Genesis-creation coherence the hymn that follows will make explicit.

echoes.text: God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, “Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.
echoes.note: The post-flood renewal of the be-fruitful-and-multiply command (also 9:7) reinforces the Genesis fruitfulness lexeme behind v.6's worldwide growth of the gospel. Recurrence of the same blessing-formula in Genesis strengthens availability; lower volume than 1:28 since the wording is the same mandate repeated.

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: The 'word of the truth of the gospel' that 'has come to you' and is fruitful in all the world echoes Isaiah's word that goes out from God's mouth and does not return empty but accomplishes and prospers, like rain making the earth bring forth and sprout. Coherence is strong: a divine word personified as agriculturally fruitful and unfailingly effective.

echoes.text: I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they shall be fruitful and multiply.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's promise that the gathered remnant 'shall be fruitful and multiply' fuses the Genesis blessing with restoration hope; Colossians' worldwide fruitful word may stand in this prophetic stream of fruitfulness-as-restoration. Faint and overlapping with the Genesis echoes, hence contested.

echoes.text: They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth will be full of the knowledge of Yahweh, as the waters cover the sea.
echoes.note: The motif of 'all the world' / earth filled (here with the fruitful word) faintly recalls Isaiah's eschatological 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea,' which also surfaces in the knowledge-language of v.9-10. Low volume, flagged contested.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The prayer to be 'filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding' (v.9) draws on the messianic endowment of Isaiah 11:2, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and knowledge. The triad wisdom/understanding/knowledge clusters in both texts, a coherent Spirit-given cognition of God's will.

echoes.text: and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,
echoes.note: Being 'filled with' wisdom and understanding (v.9) echoes Bezalel filled with the Spirit of God 'in wisdom, in understanding, and in knowledge' for the work of the sanctuary. The fullness-of-Spirit-wisdom idiom and the same three faculties make this a strong lexical parallel; availability in Exodus is secure.

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: Being delivered 'out of the power of darkness' and translated into the kingdom (v.13) draws on Isaiah's people walking in darkness who see a great light and the dawning kingdom of the messianic son (9:6-7). Light/darkness reversal plus an established kingdom of a royal son cohere tightly.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: 'The kingdom of the Son of his love' (v.13) evokes the royal-adoption oracle 'You are my Son'; with v.15-18's firstborn language it situates Christ in the Davidic sonship of Psalm 2. Volume here is thematic (beloved royal son enthroned over a kingdom) rather than verbal.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'The Son of his love' / the Beloved (v.13) carries the Aqedah resonance of Isaac, 'your son, your only son, whom you love,' a beloved-son figure offered up. Coherence with the redemption-through-death theme that immediately follows (v.14, v.20) strengthens the figural reading of the beloved son.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: 'In whom we have our redemption' after being delivered out of the domain of darkness (v.13-14) replays the exodus pattern: God redeems (apolytrosis/lytrosis) Israel out of bondage with an outstretched arm. The deliverance-then-redemption sequence and transfer into God's kingdom map onto the exodus from Egypt's darkness.

echoes.text: And with you is wisdom, which knows your works, And was present when you were making the world, And which understands what is pleasing in your eyes, And what is right according to your commandments. Send her forth out of the holy heavens, And from the throne of your glory bid her come, That being present with me she may toil with me, And that I may learn what is well-pleasing before you. For she knows all things and has understanding thereof, And in my […]
echoes.note: Solomon's prayer that Wisdom be sent to teach 'what is pleasing' to God and to guide him to 'walk' rightly parallels v.9-10's prayer for knowledge of God's will so as to 'walk worthily... pleasing him.' The walk/please/wisdom cluster is Wisdom-tradition coherent, though diffuse.

echoes.text: But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.
echoes.note: The 'inheritance of the saints in light' (v.12) faintly recalls Daniel's promise that the wise will 'rest and stand in your allotted inheritance at the end of days' and shine like the brightness of the firmament (12:3). The lot/inheritance of the holy ones in light is apocalyptic-coherent. Faint, contested.

echoes.text: How was he counted among sons of God? And how is his lot among saints?
echoes.note: 'The inheritance of the saints in light' (v.12) resonates with Wisdom 5:5, where the righteous are numbered 'among the sons of God' and their 'lot is among the saints/holy ones.' Shared lot-among-the-holy-ones language gives modest coherence with Second-Temple beatific-portion expectation.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill.
echoes.note: 'Son of his love' (v.13) may faintly echo Isaiah's 'song of my beloved' for the vineyard; the LXX agapetos vocabulary links beloved-son and beloved-vineyard traditions. Low volume and contested against the stronger Psalm 2 / Genesis 22 candidates.

echoes.text: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine.
echoes.note: 'Our redemption, the forgiveness of sins' (v.14) resonates with Isaiah's 'I have redeemed you, I have called you by name, you are mine,' and 43:25's blotting out of transgressions. Redemption coupled with forgiveness is a second-exodus motif; volume modest, flagged contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.”
echoes.note: The 'power of darkness' from which we are delivered (v.13) may glance at the plague of palpable darkness over Egypt that the exodus undoes, reinforcing the deliverance-from-darkness-into-kingdom exodus typology. Faint and contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The lawyer's answer cites the Shema's command to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and strength, the heart of Israel's covenant confession. This is a near-verbatim quotation (Luke adds mind), unmistakable in volume and availability.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: And your neighbor as yourself quotes verbatim the Holiness Code's neighbor-love command, which then drives the Who is my neighbor question. The exact wording and its programmatic role make this a clear quotation.

echoes.text: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Do this, and you will live echoes the Levitical promise that the one who keeps God's statutes shall live by them, framing eternal life as covenant obedience. The do-them-and-live formula is distinctive enough to register as an allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: The promise that God will circumcise the heart so Israel may love the LORD with all heart and soul stands behind the wholehearted love demanded here. It is a faint reinforcing echo of the Deuteronomic love-command cluster.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Inherit eternal life draws on the only clear OT promise of everlasting life, where some awake to everlasting life. The phrase supplies the eschatological referent though the contact is conceptual rather than verbal.

echoes.text: The men who have been mentioned by name rose up, and took the captives, and with the plunder clothed all who were naked among them, dressed them, gave them sandals, and gave them something to eat and to drink, anointed them, carried all the feeble of them on donkeys, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria.
echoes.note: The compassionate Samaritan who binds wounds, anoints with oil, sets the man on his own animal, and brings him to care closely mirrors the men of Samaria who clothed, anointed, carried on donkeys, and brought the Judean captives to Jericho. The cluster of shared details (Samaritans, oil/anointing, animal, conveying the helpless toward Jericho) is too dense to be coincidental.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them, ‘A priest shall not defile himself for the dead among his people; except for his relatives that are near to him: for his mother, for his father, for his son, for his daughter, for his brother, and for his virgin sister who is near to him, who has had no husband; for her he may defile himself.
echoes.note: The priest passing by on the other side gains its edge from the priestly prohibition against defilement by a corpse, since the victim appeared half dead. The corpse-purity background coheres with the priest's and Levite's avoidance, sharpening the parable's irony.

echoes.text: “He who touches the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days. He shall purify himself with water on the third day, and on the seventh day he shall be clean; but if he doesn’t purify himself the third day, then the seventh day he shall not be clean. Whoever touches a dead person, the body of a man who has died, and doesn’t purify himself, defiles Yahweh’s tabernacle; and that soul shall be cut off from Israel; because the water for impurity was not […]
echoes.note: The general corpse-impurity law (seven-day uncleanness from touching a dead body) reinforces the ritual motive a priest and Levite might invoke for keeping their distance. It supplies recurrence to the purity rationale behind the passing by.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: The verdict that the neighbor is the one who showed mercy embodies Hosea's I desire mercy and not sacrifice, prioritizing compassion over the cultic scruples of priest and Levite. The mercy-over-cult coherence with the parable's structure supports the allusion.

echoes.text: From the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness in it: wounds, welts, and open sores. They haven’t been closed, neither bandaged, neither soothed with oil.
echoes.note: Pouring oil and wine on wounds faintly recalls Isaiah's image of wounds not pressed out or softened with oil, the standard idiom for medicinal care. The contact is on the treatment imagery only and remains low-confidence.

notes.text: For good — Whereas thou did formerly receive these mercies for thy hurt, now thou shalt have them for thy good, thy heart shall be so changed that thou shalt not now abuse them, but employ them to the service of God the giver. Over thee for good - To do thee good; as he did rejoice to destroy thee.

If thou wilt hearken — This is added to warn them that they should not receive the grace of God in vain, and to teach them that the grace of God doth not discharge man's obligation to his duty, nor excuse him for the neglect of it. It is observable, that Moses calls God, the Lord thy God twelve times in these ten verses. In the threatnings of the former chapter, he is all along called the Lord, a God of power, and the judge of all. But in the promises of this chapter, the Lord thy God, a God of grace, and in covenant with thee.

This commandment — The great command of loving and obeying God, which is the sum of the law, of which yet he doth not here speak, as it is in itself, but as it is molified and accompanied with the grace of the gospel. The meaning is, that tho' the practice of God's laws be now far from us, and above our strength, yet, considering the advantage of gospel grace, whereby God enables us to do our duty, it is near and easy to us, who believe. And so this well agrees with Rom. x, 6, &c. where St. Paul applies this place to the righteousness of faith. Is not hidden - Hebrew. Is not too wonderful for thee, not too hard for thee to know and do. The will of God, which is but darkly manifested to other nations, Acts xvii, 27, is clearly and fully revealed unto thee: thou canst not pretend ignorance or invincible difficulty.
In heaven — Shut up there, but it hath been thence delivered and published in thy hearing.

Neither beyond the sea — The knowledge of this commandment is not to be fetched from far distant places, to which divers of the wise Heathens travelled for their wisdom; but it was brought to thy very doors and ears, and declared to thee in this wilderness.

In thy mouth — Thou knowest it so well, that it is the matter of thy common discourse. In thy heart - In thy mind, (as the heart is very commonly taken) to understand and believe it. In a word, the Law is plain and easy: but the gospel is much more so.

glossa.text: *This commandment, which I,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 54.)) LXX: *For this commandment,* etc., *as far as* without which, if they be done outwardly with the hands and be not done in the heart, the precepts of God are not fulfilled.

*The word is nigh thee,* etc. That is, the commandments of God are measured and tempered to human strength. This can be taken of the incarnation of Christ, who, having assumed humanity, was seen upon earth and conversed among men.

notes.text: Ashamed — Disappointed of my hope.
Cause — Without any provocation of mine.
Teach — Teach me my duty, and cause me to keep close to it, notwithstanding all temptations.
Upright — Holy and true, in all his declarations and offers of mercy to sinners. Therefore - He will not be wanting to such poor sinners as I am, but will guide them into the way of life and peace.
The meek — Such as meekly submit themselves to God, and are desirous to be directed and governed by him. Judgment - In the paths of judgment, in the right way.
Paths — All the dealings of God with them, yea even those that are afflictive, are done in kindness and faithfulness to them.

glossa.text:
*Unto the end.* ((Hier.)) Here the penitent who has been scourged is set before the rest, lest they murmur in adversities: he who, having had the trial in himself, coaxes through mercy and terrifies through justice.

 *To thee, O Lord, have I lifted up.* ((AUG.)) A psalm against the adversities of the world, etc., *as far as* who not through all, the less perfect.

((CASS.)) First he asks to be taught the ways of the Lord, because he is raised up toward God.

((ID.)) Toward the contemplating of thee; he easily despises earthly things who beholds things divine.

*I trust.* ((ID.)) Having had trial of my own weakness in evils, I shall not blush because of my enemies.

*Neither let my enemies laugh at me:* and I am sure that he deceives none that endures patiently.

*In vain.* ((ID.)) Because all things are vain and unfruitful which are alien from God.

*Shew me thy ways, O Lord.* ((CASS.)) The ways are of the order of life, etc., *as far as: Direct,* belongs to life, *teach* to knowledge.

*Teach.* ((AUG.)) Truth itself, that I may understand what I believe, because I have endured; and if this suffices not: *Remember.*

*God my saviour.* ((CASS.)) There are two things which make men good, that we believe God our saviour, and that we patiently await his retribution.

*Remember.* ((ID.)) Of former sins and of those which are daily done, he prays through the mercy shewn to the ancients, and because he fears a true judge.

*Of thy tender mercies.* Compassion is properly in the shewing forth of good things.

*Which are from of old.* ((AUG.)) That is, they are from the beginning of the world: therefore let him not fail in me.

*Sins.* ((CASS.)) They are when the way of equity is forsaken.

*Of my youth.* Not for age, but for the rashness of headlong haste, which is then, when the heat of the mind exceeds moderation.

*Ignorances.* We do those things which we do not know to be evil. Or the sins of ignorance in little ones, who are held at any rate by original sin.

((HIER.)) Of my youth. Before I went out of the house of my wicked father.

*Remember me, thou.* ((AUG.)) Whose work it is to have mercy and to forgive sins.

*According to thy mercy.* That is, thy mercy is ample. Mercy is toward the wretched, goodness toward any whatsoever. But God does good both when implored by the wretched, and when led by his goodness: none is good but God.

*Sweet.* ((ID.)) Because he forgives all former things, where grace is without merits.

*Right.* Because after mercy, etc., *as far as Sweet,* because he gives sweet things; *right,* because he corrects.

*Therefore.* ((CASS.)) Because he is sweet and right; not out of cruelty, but out of kindness.

*In the way.* That is, faith, or the precepts of God. Or in the way of this life, where one must live rightly, he will give a law.

*In judgment.* While he punishes, he will direct to better things. But let them be meek who are corrected: for from wild beasts they are tamed, that they may bear it. For if they are mild, that is, of a gentle mind, as though having this by nature: he will teach them the precepts for the neglect of which came the scourges.

*Mercy and truth.* ((AUG.)) But what ways he will teach, etc., *as far as* and then he guards against the severity of the judge.

*Testament.* ((CASS.)) The New, which is excellently called a Testament, where there is a clear and certain promise of an inheritance, which is confirmed by death also.

*And the Testament.* Of the old law, where the Prophets were witnesses of the promises.

notes.text: Commends the knowledge of Christ, as more excellent than all other, and so entire and perfect that no other knowledge was necessary for a Christian. He shows,

That Christ is above all angels, who are only his servants; and that, being reconciled to God through him, we have free access to him in all our necessities. This epistle contains, I. The inscription, Chap. i. 1, 2 II. The doctrine, wherein the apostle pathetically explains the mystery of Christ, By thanksgiving for the Colossians, 3-8 By prayers for them, 9-23 With a declaration of his affection for them, 24-29 ii. 1-3 III. The exhortation,

1. General, wherein he excites them to perseverance, and warns them not to be deceived, 4-8 Describes again the mystery of Christ in order, 9-15 And in the same order, draws his admonitions,

1. From Christ the head, 16-19

2. From his death, 20-23

3. From his exaltation, iii. 1-4

2. Particular, 5-9

1. To avoid several vices,

2. To practice several virtues, 10, 11 Especially to love one another, 12-15 And study the scriptures 16, 17

3. To the relative duties of wives and husbands,. 18, 19 Children and parents, 20, 21 Servants and masters, 22-25 iv.1 Final, to prayer, 2-4 to spiritual wisdom 5, 6 V. The conclusion, 7-16 COLOSSIANS
We give thanks — There is a near resemblance between this epistle, and those to the Ephesians and Philippians.
Ye heard before — I wrote to you. In the word of truth, of the gospel - The true gospel preached to you.
It bringeth forth fruit in all the world — That is, in every place where it is preached. Ye knew the grace of God in truth - Truly experienced the gracious power of God.
The fellowservant — Of Paul and Timotheus.
Your love in the Spirit — Your love wrought in you by the Spirit.

We pray for you — This was mentioned in general, Colossians i, 3, but now more particularly. That ye may be filled with the knowledge of his will - Of his revealed will. In all wisdom - With all the wisdom from above. And spiritual understanding - To discern by that light whatever agrees with, or differs from, his will.

That, knowing his whole will, ye may walk worthy of the Lord, unto all pleasing — So as actually to please him in all things; daily increasing in the living, experimental knowledge of God, our Father, saviour, Sanctifier.

Strengthened unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness — This is the highest point: not only to know, to do, to suffer, the whole will of God; but to suffer it to the end, not barely with patience, but with thankful joy.
Who, by justifying and sanctifying us, hath made us meet for glory.
Power detains reluctant captives, a kingdom cherishes willing subjects. His beloved Son — This is treated of in the fifteenth and following verses.

In whom we have redemption — This is treated of from the middle of Colossians i, 18. The voluntary passion of our Lord appeased the Father's wrath, obtained pardon and acceptance for us, and, consequently, dissolved the dominion and power which Satan had over us through our sins. So that forgiveness is the beginning of redemption, as the resurrection is the completion of it.

glossa.text: *Paul.* After his custom he sets the salutation first. This being set first, he gives thanks for their good things, and, commending their faith and love, he prays that they may be made perfect in Christ, whose benefits and primacy he commends according to both natures; then, calling to mind the dignity of his own ministry, he admonishes them not to withdraw from Christ, seduced through prophecy or the ceremonies of the law; last of all he instructs all together, morally, according to sexes and ages and conditions, and at the end he warns Archippus that he is to be careful of the ministry he has undertaken. *An apostle,* etc. Note that to all in dignity he here rightly names himself an apostle, because he was an apostle to these also, to whom he had preached through his own disciples.
*We give thanks.* He shows the good things which they received, while he gives thanks for them.

*As,* etc. That is, so purely and truly as it came through me and others into the whole world, and still remains in it, as if he should say: Not less has been done for you than in the other churches. Since the Gospel is in the world, it bears fruit there through good works, and grows by the increase of knowledge and by the number of the faithful. Not by this do they have more than you, but God does this in the same manner as it is among you, and therefore you ought to add nothing further.
*For you,* etc. Desiring whose salvation, he began to help Archippus.
*In the Spirit.* Because you love for spiritual things, not for carnal.
*That you may be filled in all.* It is a great thing to know fully what God wills, in all the matters of the active and the contemplative life.
*In knowledge.* That they may not be ignorant of the form of their faith, that is, of the thing hoped for, whence they will be firm.

*In all virtue.* You, I say, strengthened by God in all virtue, namely chastity and the rest. Which he can well do who is the brightness of the Father, that is, the Son. Or according as he has given you clear knowledge.

*Giving thanks.* Now he begins to say that the law does not profit but harms, and that Christ suffices for all good things: which can be known from this, that he himself and the other apostles (who had been in the observances of the law), having dismissed them, fled for refuge to Christ: As if he should say: We pray for you, giving thanks to God, for this reason, because he makes us worthy, which the law never could.

 *He has made us worthy.* Not in the law, but *in the light,* that is, through God who is light of light, by whose grace we are illumined. Or *in the light,* that is, in clear knowledge, from which he who turns aside falls into darkness. *Of the lot.* The will of God is the lot in the human race, with whom there is no iniquity, but he does all things by justice, though a hidden one.

*He has snatched us from the power.* That is, from hell, in which we were held by the devil: as much from our own transgression as from Adam's. *And has translated,* etc. When, raising us from the depth of Tartarus, he brought us into heaven with his only Son. For now believers, who are devoted with fixed mind, going forth from the world, are brought into heaven with an angel of the Father's right hand for their guide. *The kingdom of the Son.* Of which he himself says: *My kingdom is not of this world;* he did not say: It is not here, but, *it is not hence,* because he does indeed sojourn in the world, but is not of the world. For to his own kingdom he says, *You are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world.* They were of the world, when they belonged to the prince of the world.

*Redemption.* The power of the devil being destroyed, the means of liberty was given to us by the pouring out of the blood of him who had no sin. So that, because the devil justly held those whom, guilty of sin, he had bound by the condition of death, he might justly let these go through him whom, guilty of no sin, the punishment of death undeservedly visited.

notes.text: Matt. xxii, 35; Mark xii, 28.

Thou shalt love the Lord thy God — That is, thou shalt unite all the faculties of thy soul to render him the most intelligent and sincere, the most affectionate and resolute service. We may safely rest in this general sense of these important words, if we are not able to fix the particular meaning of every single word. If we desire to do this, perhaps the heart, which is a general expression, may be explained by the three following, With all thy soul, with the warmest affection, with all thy strength, the most vigourous efforts of thy will, and with all thy mind or understanding, in the most wise and reasonable manner thou canst; thy understanding guiding thy will and affections. Deut. vi, 5; Lev. xix, 18.

Thou hast answered right; this do, and thou shalt live — Here is no irony, but a deep and weighty truth. He, and he alone, shall live forever, who thus loves God and his neighbour in the present life.
To justify himself — That is, to show he had done this. Lev. xviii, 5.

From Jerusalem to Jericho — The road from Jerusalem to Jericho (about eighteen miles from it) lay through desert and rocky places: so many robberies and murders were committed therein, that it was called the bloody way. Jericho was situated in the valley: hence the phrase of going down to it. About twelve thousand priests and Levites dwelt there, who all attended the service of the temple.

The common translation is, by chance — Which is full of gross improprieties. For if we speak strictly, there is no such thing in the universe as either chance or fortune. A certain priest came down that way, and passed by on the other side - And both he and the Levite no doubt could find an excuse for passing over on the other side, and might perhaps gravely thank God for their own deliverance, while they left their brother bleeding to death. Is it not an emblem of many living characters, perhaps of some who bear the sacred office? O house of Levi and of Aaron, is not the day coming, when the virtues of heathens and Samaritans will rise up in judgment against you?

But a certain Samaritan came where he was — It was admirably well judged to represent the distress on the side of the Jew, and the mercy on that of the Samaritan. For the case being thus proposed, self interest would make the very scribe sensible, how amiable such a conduct was, and would lay him open to our Lord's inference. Had it been put the other way, prejudice might more easily have interposed, before the heart could have been affected.
Pouring in oil and wine — Which when well beaten together are one of the best balsams that can be applied to a fresh wound.
Which of these was the neighbour to him that fell among the robbers — Which acted the part of a neighbour?

And he said, He that showed mercy on him — He could not for shame say otherwise, though he thereby condemned himself and overthrew his own false notion of the neighbour to whom our love is due. Go and do thou in like manner - Let us go and do likewise, regarding every man as our neighbour who needs our assistance. Let us renounce that bigotry and party zeal which would contract our hearts into an insensibility for all the human race, but a small number whose sentiments and practices are so much our own, that our love to them is but self love reflected. With an honest openness of mind let us always remember that kindred between man and man, and cultivate that happy instinct whereby, in the original constitution of our nature, God has strongly bound us to each other.

glossa.text: *A lawyer stood up.* The doctor of the law, who was lying in the law without faith, rises that he may stand: he stands while he calls him Master, but even in standing he tempts God by keeping silent about what he was.
*He answering said.* He said what he had read, but did not fulfil what was written, because he had present with him the Lord whom he ought to love, yet he calls him Master, not God.

*But he, willing.* The lawyer, that he may be said to have answered wisely, first confesses that he is ignorant of the commandment of the law, because, refusing to be humbled and willing to justify himself, he cannot see the hidden things that are revealed to the little ones of Christ; to whom Christ so tempers his answer that both everyone who does mercy may be understood to be a neighbour, and especially the Son of God himself, who through his humanity has been made neighbour to us, may be designated. *Who is my.* No one is nearer to man than God, who knows him within and without and can care for all things; but every unbeliever or tempter has neither God nor man for a neighbour.

*A certain man,* etc. ((AUG.)) That man is understood to be Adam in the human race, etc., *as far as* he was nearer than the priest or the Levite of the same nation.

*And it happened,* etc. The priest announces the law of God: the law indeed came down through Moses into the world, and conferred no health upon such a one. The Levite came down, who shows the type of the prophets, but he too heals no one, because the law reproves sins, but passes by, since it does not bestow pardon.
*Being moved with mercy.* This is not said of the priest and the Levite, because the law has not mercy, but judgment and vengeance.
*He brought him to an inn.* He calls it not a house but a stable, by which name he marks the miseries and the stenches of this life, lest a man rejoice in this exile as though in his fatherland.
*He that did.* Kinship does not make a neighbour, but mercy, which mercy is according to nature. For nothing is so according to nature as to help a partner of one's nature.

echoes.text: Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
echoes.note: The epistolary blessing 'Grace to you and peace' channels the Aaronic benediction's pairing of divine favor and shalom (the LORD make his face shine... and give you peace). Volume is low and the formula is conventionally Pauline, but the coherence with the priestly grace/peace dyad and its availability in the Torah make it a plausible faint figural backdrop.

echoes.text: God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
echoes.note: The gospel 'bearing fruit and growing... in all the world' (v.6) replays the creation/Edenic mandate 'be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.' The paired participles fruit-bearing + increasing, set worldwide, deliberately recast the protological blessing as the spread of the word, a Genesis-creation coherence the hymn that follows will make explicit.

echoes.text: God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, “Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.
echoes.note: The post-flood renewal of the be-fruitful-and-multiply command (also 9:7) reinforces the Genesis fruitfulness lexeme behind v.6's worldwide growth of the gospel. Recurrence of the same blessing-formula in Genesis strengthens availability; lower volume than 1:28 since the wording is the same mandate repeated.

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: The 'word of the truth of the gospel' that 'has come to you' and is fruitful in all the world echoes Isaiah's word that goes out from God's mouth and does not return empty but accomplishes and prospers, like rain making the earth bring forth and sprout. Coherence is strong: a divine word personified as agriculturally fruitful and unfailingly effective.

echoes.text: I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they shall be fruitful and multiply.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's promise that the gathered remnant 'shall be fruitful and multiply' fuses the Genesis blessing with restoration hope; Colossians' worldwide fruitful word may stand in this prophetic stream of fruitfulness-as-restoration. Faint and overlapping with the Genesis echoes, hence contested.

echoes.text: They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth will be full of the knowledge of Yahweh, as the waters cover the sea.
echoes.note: The motif of 'all the world' / earth filled (here with the fruitful word) faintly recalls Isaiah's eschatological 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea,' which also surfaces in the knowledge-language of v.9-10. Low volume, flagged contested.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: The prayer to be 'filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding' (v.9) draws on the messianic endowment of Isaiah 11:2, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and knowledge. The triad wisdom/understanding/knowledge clusters in both texts, a coherent Spirit-given cognition of God's will.

echoes.text: and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,
echoes.note: Being 'filled with' wisdom and understanding (v.9) echoes Bezalel filled with the Spirit of God 'in wisdom, in understanding, and in knowledge' for the work of the sanctuary. The fullness-of-Spirit-wisdom idiom and the same three faculties make this a strong lexical parallel; availability in Exodus is secure.

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: Being delivered 'out of the power of darkness' and translated into the kingdom (v.13) draws on Isaiah's people walking in darkness who see a great light and the dawning kingdom of the messianic son (9:6-7). Light/darkness reversal plus an established kingdom of a royal son cohere tightly.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: 'The kingdom of the Son of his love' (v.13) evokes the royal-adoption oracle 'You are my Son'; with v.15-18's firstborn language it situates Christ in the Davidic sonship of Psalm 2. Volume here is thematic (beloved royal son enthroned over a kingdom) rather than verbal.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'The Son of his love' / the Beloved (v.13) carries the Aqedah resonance of Isaac, 'your son, your only son, whom you love,' a beloved-son figure offered up. Coherence with the redemption-through-death theme that immediately follows (v.14, v.20) strengthens the figural reading of the beloved son.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: 'In whom we have our redemption' after being delivered out of the domain of darkness (v.13-14) replays the exodus pattern: God redeems (apolytrosis/lytrosis) Israel out of bondage with an outstretched arm. The deliverance-then-redemption sequence and transfer into God's kingdom map onto the exodus from Egypt's darkness.

echoes.text: And with you is wisdom, which knows your works, And was present when you were making the world, And which understands what is pleasing in your eyes, And what is right according to your commandments. Send her forth out of the holy heavens, And from the throne of your glory bid her come, That being present with me she may toil with me, And that I may learn what is well-pleasing before you. For she knows all things and has understanding thereof, And in my […]
echoes.note: Solomon's prayer that Wisdom be sent to teach 'what is pleasing' to God and to guide him to 'walk' rightly parallels v.9-10's prayer for knowledge of God's will so as to 'walk worthily... pleasing him.' The walk/please/wisdom cluster is Wisdom-tradition coherent, though diffuse.

echoes.text: But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.
echoes.note: The 'inheritance of the saints in light' (v.12) faintly recalls Daniel's promise that the wise will 'rest and stand in your allotted inheritance at the end of days' and shine like the brightness of the firmament (12:3). The lot/inheritance of the holy ones in light is apocalyptic-coherent. Faint, contested.

echoes.text: How was he counted among sons of God? And how is his lot among saints?
echoes.note: 'The inheritance of the saints in light' (v.12) resonates with Wisdom 5:5, where the righteous are numbered 'among the sons of God' and their 'lot is among the saints/holy ones.' Shared lot-among-the-holy-ones language gives modest coherence with Second-Temple beatific-portion expectation.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill.
echoes.note: 'Son of his love' (v.13) may faintly echo Isaiah's 'song of my beloved' for the vineyard; the LXX agapetos vocabulary links beloved-son and beloved-vineyard traditions. Low volume and contested against the stronger Psalm 2 / Genesis 22 candidates.

echoes.text: But now thus says Yahweh who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine.
echoes.note: 'Our redemption, the forgiveness of sins' (v.14) resonates with Isaiah's 'I have redeemed you, I have called you by name, you are mine,' and 43:25's blotting out of transgressions. Redemption coupled with forgiveness is a second-exodus motif; volume modest, flagged contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt.”
echoes.note: The 'power of darkness' from which we are delivered (v.13) may glance at the plague of palpable darkness over Egypt that the exodus undoes, reinforcing the deliverance-from-darkness-into-kingdom exodus typology. Faint and contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The lawyer's answer cites the Shema's command to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and strength, the heart of Israel's covenant confession. This is a near-verbatim quotation (Luke adds mind), unmistakable in volume and availability.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: And your neighbor as yourself quotes verbatim the Holiness Code's neighbor-love command, which then drives the Who is my neighbor question. The exact wording and its programmatic role make this a clear quotation.

echoes.text: You shall therefore keep my statutes and my ordinances; which if a man does, he shall live in them. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: Do this, and you will live echoes the Levitical promise that the one who keeps God's statutes shall live by them, framing eternal life as covenant obedience. The do-them-and-live formula is distinctive enough to register as an allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your seed, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.
echoes.note: The promise that God will circumcise the heart so Israel may love the LORD with all heart and soul stands behind the wholehearted love demanded here. It is a faint reinforcing echo of the Deuteronomic love-command cluster.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: Inherit eternal life draws on the only clear OT promise of everlasting life, where some awake to everlasting life. The phrase supplies the eschatological referent though the contact is conceptual rather than verbal.

echoes.text: The men who have been mentioned by name rose up, and took the captives, and with the plunder clothed all who were naked among them, dressed them, gave them sandals, and gave them something to eat and to drink, anointed them, carried all the feeble of them on donkeys, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria.
echoes.note: The compassionate Samaritan who binds wounds, anoints with oil, sets the man on his own animal, and brings him to care closely mirrors the men of Samaria who clothed, anointed, carried on donkeys, and brought the Judean captives to Jericho. The cluster of shared details (Samaritans, oil/anointing, animal, conveying the helpless toward Jericho) is too dense to be coincidental.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them, ‘A priest shall not defile himself for the dead among his people; except for his relatives that are near to him: for his mother, for his father, for his son, for his daughter, for his brother, and for his virgin sister who is near to him, who has had no husband; for her he may defile himself.
echoes.note: The priest passing by on the other side gains its edge from the priestly prohibition against defilement by a corpse, since the victim appeared half dead. The corpse-purity background coheres with the priest's and Levite's avoidance, sharpening the parable's irony.

echoes.text: “He who touches the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days. He shall purify himself with water on the third day, and on the seventh day he shall be clean; but if he doesn’t purify himself the third day, then the seventh day he shall not be clean. Whoever touches a dead person, the body of a man who has died, and doesn’t purify himself, defiles Yahweh’s tabernacle; and that soul shall be cut off from Israel; because the water for impurity was not […]
echoes.note: The general corpse-impurity law (seven-day uncleanness from touching a dead body) reinforces the ritual motive a priest and Levite might invoke for keeping their distance. It supplies recurrence to the purity rationale behind the passing by.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: The verdict that the neighbor is the one who showed mercy embodies Hosea's I desire mercy and not sacrifice, prioritizing compassion over the cultic scruples of priest and Levite. The mercy-over-cult coherence with the parable's structure supports the allusion.

echoes.text: From the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness in it: wounds, welts, and open sores. They haven’t been closed, neither bandaged, neither soothed with oil.
echoes.note: Pouring oil and wine on wounds faintly recalls Isaiah's image of wounds not pressed out or softened with oil, the standard idiom for medicinal care. The contact is on the treatment imagery only and remains low-confidence.

registers.label: Spare
lines: God stands among us with a plumb line, measuring what we have built.
Set our crooked walls true, O Lord.
A man lay wounded on the Jericho road, and a stranger stopped.
Mercy bent down, poured oil on the wounds, and carried him home.
Give justice to the weak; rescue the lowly and the poor.
This is the worship God asks of us.
Come, and learn to love your neighbor.
Go, and do likewise. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture the road down to Jericho — dust, heat, a man beaten and left in the ditch, and the footsteps of the religious passing by on the far side.
Lord, teach us to do likewise.
Then an outsider, a Samaritan, kneels in the dirt, pours oil and wine into the wounds, lifts him onto his own animal, and pays his way.
Lord, teach us to do likewise.
God holds a plumb line against our lives and asks for justice — defend the weak, lift the fallen, do not look away.
Lord, teach us to do likewise.
So come in from your own long road, be tended and healed, and go back out as neighbor to the next one in the ditch.
Lord, teach us to do likewise. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: God holds a plumb line to all we have built.
Go, and do likewise.
A stranger knelt and poured oil on the wounds.
Go, and do likewise.
Justice for the weak is the worship God wants.
Go, and do likewise.
Come, love your neighbor, and then go.
Go, and do likewise. Amen.
